prompt: A launch template has versions 1 to 3. Somebody needs version 2 to have a larger root volume. What do they do?
hint: What happens to a version once it is written?

choices.text: Edit version 2 in place; groups pick it up at their next launch
choices.why: A version is immutable on AWS. There is no call that edits one; the change has to be a new version.

choices.text: Delete version 2 and create it again under the same number
choices.why: Numbers are not reused. Deleting version 2 leaves a gap, and the next version created is 4.

choices.text: Resize the volume on an instance, which writes it back into version 2
choices.why: Nothing flows from an instance back into a template. The instance changes and the version stays as it was written.

choices.text: Create version 4 with the bigger disk, and point whatever should use it at 4
choices.why: Right. Versions are never edited, only added (or deleted), so the fix is the next number, and whatever should use it is pointed at 4.

prompt: A group says Version=$Latest. A colleague creates version 5 to try a new image and does not touch the default. What happens?
hint: Which of the two names moves by itself?

choices.text: Nothing until somebody runs modify-launch-template --default-version 5
choices.why: That is how $Default moves. $Latest follows the highest number, so it already means 5.

choices.text: Every running instance is replaced by one from version 5 straight away
choices.why: A version change touches no running instance. Replacing them is a separate act, such as an instance refresh.

choices.text: The group's next launch, whatever causes it, uses version 5
choices.why: Right. A scale-out or a replacement launched after version 5 exists resolves $Latest to 5, and the experiment is now in the group.

choices.text: The group stops launching until version 5 has been made the default
choices.why: A group does not compare $Latest with $Default; it resolves the name it was given and launches.

prompt: In the lab, a version made with --source-version 1 and only an instance type comes back holding only InstanceType. What would AWS store for it?
hint: What is --source-version for?

choices.text: Version 1's image, disk, metadata options and tags, with t3.medium as the type
choices.why: Right. On AWS the source version is copied and the data sent beside it overrides it. moto 5.2.3 ignores the source.

choices.text: The same as moto: a version keeps only what the call sent, and the source is a label
choices.why: That is moto's behaviour, and the lesson marks it as moto's. On AWS the source is what the new version is built from.

choices.text: Nothing: the call fails, because every version has to name its own image
choices.why: A version may omit the image; with a source version it inherits it, and without one it simply has none.

choices.text: Version 1's data unchanged, because the data sent is ignored when a source is named
choices.why: It is the other way round: the data sent is what changes, and everything else comes from the source.

prompt: A launch template version can be deleted, but once it exists it can never be ___.
hint: The reason a fix is always a new number.

prompt: Which of these does a launch template version hold? Choose all that apply.
hint: What one instance is, against how many there are.

choices.text: The image id
choices.why: Every launch needs one, and the template is where it is written.

choices.text: HttpTokens set to required
choices.why: Metadata options are part of what an instance is; lesson 7 explains this one.

choices.text: The minimum and maximum number of instances
choices.why: Counts belong to the group that launches from the template, not to the template.

choices.text: A 20 GB gp3 root volume deleted on termination
choices.why: Block device mappings are in the template, which is why the disk comes out the same on every instance.

choices.text: The desired capacity a scaling policy moves
choices.why: The desired capacity is the group's, and the policies of lesson 5 move it there.

choices.text: A tag put on every instance it launches
choices.why: TagSpecifications tag what is launched, which is how instances with chosen-by-nobody ids are found.

prompt: What is a group's desired capacity?
hint: Which of the three numbers do policies move?

choices.text: The count the group is working towards now, between its minimum and maximum
choices.why: Right. It sits between the minimum and the maximum, and it is the number a person or a policy moves.

choices.text: The number of instances running at this moment
choices.why: They can differ: while instances launch or terminate, what exists lags behind what is desired.

choices.text: The most instances the group will run, whatever the load
choices.why: That is the maximum, the ceiling on capacity and on the bill.

choices.text: A suggestion from a policy, which the group follows only above its minimum and only when the instances are healthy
choices.why: The group follows it whatever the health of its instances; unhealthy ones are replaced precisely to reach it.

prompt: On AWS, what happens to set-desired-capacity 8 on a group whose maximum is 6?
hint: moto accepted it. Does AWS?

choices.text: It launches eight, as moto did, and raises the maximum to match
choices.why: A maximum that moved itself would be no ceiling on the bill. moto's eight is a record nobody pays for.

choices.text: It launches six and holds the desired at eight until the maximum rises
choices.why: The desired capacity cannot sit outside the bounds. The call is refused rather than half applied.

choices.text: It refuses the call with a ValidationError, and launches nothing
choices.why: Right. The desired capacity must lie between the minimum and the maximum, and nothing is launched.

choices.text: It accepts the number and waits for a policy to confirm it
choices.why: Policies and manual calls both set the same number; neither waits for the other.

prompt: A group's desired capacity drops by one. Put the steps of AWS's default termination policy in order.
hint: Balance first.
items: Pick the zone with the most instances
Within it, prefer instances from the oldest launch template or configuration
Then prefer the instance closest to its next billing hour
Choose at random between whatever is left
trap: Starting with the oldest version would unbalance the zones, which is what the first step exists to prevent.

prompt: An instance in a group is two hours into a three-hour report. The group scales in. What keeps that instance from being the one terminated?
hint: Something that takes one instance out of the choice when the count falls.

choices.text: A health check grace period of three hours
choices.why: The grace period only stops health checks counting after launch. It plays no part in choosing whom to scale in.

choices.text: Scale-in protection on that instance
choices.why: Right. set-instance-protection removes it from the scale-in choice; a failed health check would still replace it.

choices.text: A tag such as keep=true on the instance
choices.why: No termination policy reads your tags. The order is zone, template age, billing hour, chance.

choices.text: Suspending the group's HealthCheck process
choices.why: That stops health checks, not scale-in. The group would still pick an instance to terminate.

prompt: How do you list the instances of the group web, whose ids change every time one is replaced?
hint: A tag nobody but AWS can write.

choices.text: Filter on app=shop, which the template puts on every instance
choices.why: Anybody can write app=shop, on any instance or in any other template, so it identifies a purpose and not a group.

choices.text: Keep the ids that create-auto-scaling-group printed when the group was made
choices.why: It prints nothing when it works, and the ids would be stale after the first replacement anyway.

choices.text: Filter on the tag aws:autoscaling:groupName=web, which only AWS writes
choices.why: Right. AWS writes it on every instance the group launches, and the aws: prefix is reserved for AWS alone.

choices.text: Filter on the subnets in the group's --vpc-zone-identifier
choices.why: Other instances share those subnets; a subnet says where something runs, not who launched it.

prompt: moto put every instance of a group given three subnets in three zones into sa-east-1a. What does AWS do with the same group?
hint: Why give a group more than one zone?

choices.text: The same: a group fills its first subnet before using the next
choices.why: That is moto's simplification. AWS spreads from the first launch.

choices.text: It spreads them evenly over the three zones, and keeps them even as instances come and go
choices.why: Right. One per zone for three instances, two per zone for six, so a lost zone takes a third of the group and not all of it.

choices.text: It puts each one in whichever zone has the lowest price that hour
choices.why: On-demand prices do not differ between zones of a region, and placement follows balance, not price.

choices.text: It needs --availability-zones as well, or it uses one zone like moto
choices.why: The subnets already name the zones; the group works them out, as its description showed.

prompt: A group has a maximum of 30. While AZRebalance moves instances between zones, what is the largest number of instances AWS lets it run?
hint: 10% of the maximum, or one instance, whichever is larger.

prompt: Match each setting or call to what it does about an instance's health.
hint: Two sources of answers, one pause, one manual verdict.

pairs.right: Catches a failed host or a kernel that stopped
Also catches a web server that stopped answering /health
Ignores failed checks for a while after launch
Lets a person or a script declare an instance unhealthy

right_distractors: Adds instances when the average CPU rises

prompt: A new group behind a load balancer has health check type ELB and no grace period. The application takes four minutes to start. What happens?
hint: What does the group see during those four minutes?

choices.text: Each new instance fails its check while starting, is replaced, and the loop goes on
choices.why: Right. With no grace period the first failed /health counts, so no instance lives long enough to start, and every launch is billed.

choices.text: The instances serve after four minutes, because a target group waits for new targets
choices.why: A target group marks a target unhealthy as soon as its checks fail; waiting is what the group's grace period is for.

choices.text: The group waits for the first healthy answer before it starts checking
choices.why: There is no such wait unless the grace period provides it, and here it is zero.

choices.text: The load balancer marks them unhealthy, but the group acts only on EC2 checks
choices.why: With type ELB both sources count; that is the point of setting it.

prompt: After set-instance-health --health-status Unhealthy, moto still listed the instance, running and marked Unhealthy. What would AWS have done?
hint: Replaced, not repaired.

choices.text: The same: the status is a label, and replacement waits for the next health check
choices.why: On AWS the status is the verdict itself. moto writing it down and stopping is moto's gap.

choices.text: Rebooted it, and marked it healthy again if it answered afterwards
choices.why: Groups do not reboot. Whatever was on the instance is assumed to live elsewhere, so a new one is cheaper than a repair.

choices.text: Terminated it and lowered the desired capacity by one
choices.why: Health replacement keeps the count. Lowering it is what --should-decrement-desired-capacity asks for, by hand.

choices.text: Terminated it and launched a replacement from the template
choices.why: Right. An unhealthy instance is replaced, not repaired, and the count goes back to the desired capacity.

prompt: Ana makes version 3, a t3.medium, the template's default. What happens to the three t3.micro instances already running?
hint: A template describes the next launch.

choices.text: They are stopped, changed to t3.medium and started again
choices.why: Nothing resizes them. A template is read at launch and never again.

choices.text: The group replaces them one at a time, since it follows its default
choices.why: The group follows the default for new launches only. Replacing on purpose is an instance refresh.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. Each one keeps version 1 until it is terminated for some other reason, as the transcript showed.

choices.text: They are marked unhealthy, so that health replacement brings in version 3
choices.why: An old version is not a health problem; the group has no rule that confuses the two.

prompt: A group of 20 instances is refreshed with MinHealthyPercentage 90 and InstanceWarmup 60. Each new instance takes 4 minutes to launch, boot and pass its health check. About how many minutes does the refresh take?
hint: How many may be out at once? Then batches times minutes per batch.

prompt: With ten instances and a MinHealthyPercentage of 50, an instance refresh replaces ___ instances in each batch.
hint: Half of them must stay healthy.

prompt: A refresh stopped halfway. Which preference lets you start it again without replacing the instances it already replaced?
hint: Something that compares each instance with the desired version.

choices.text: AutoRollback
choices.why: That returns the group to its previous version when a refresh fails; it is the opposite direction.

choices.text: CheckpointPercentages
choices.why: Checkpoints pause a refresh at chosen points. They do not decide which instances to skip.

choices.text: SkipMatching
choices.why: Right. Instances already on the desired template version are left alone.

choices.text: MinHealthyPercentage of 100
choices.why: That limits how many go at once, and every instance would still be replaced.

prompt: In the lab, start-instance-refresh answered with an HTML page saying 500 Internal Server Error. What does that tell you?
hint: Whose error is a 500 with an HTML body, where XML was expected?

choices.text: The preferences JSON is wrong, since AWS answers bad input with a 500
choices.why: AWS answers bad input with a 400 and a ValidationError in XML. A 500 is the server failing, whatever was sent.

choices.text: That moto does not implement the call, and nothing about what AWS would do
choices.why: Right. moto 5.2.3 has no instance refresh; the error is its own, and the request says nothing about AWS either way.

choices.text: That three instances are too few for a minimum healthy percentage of 90
choices.why: AWS replaces at least one instance at a time whatever the percentage; the size of the group does not produce a server error.

choices.text: That the template's default version is the broken version 2
choices.why: The default was 3 by then, and a refresh would not reach the template before the server failed.

prompt: On AWS, the web server on an instance in an ELB group stops answering /health. Put what follows in order.
hint: By default the old one goes before the new one comes.
items: The target group's health check fails on the instance
The group marks the instance unhealthy
The group launches a replacement from the template
After its grace period the replacement passes its checks
trap: For an unhealthy instance the group terminates first and launches second by default; it is rebalancing that launches first.

prompt: A group has minimum 2 and desired 3. You terminate one instance with --should-decrement-desired-capacity. What follows?
hint: Which number does the flag change?

choices.text: Desired falls to 2, and nothing replaces the instance
choices.why: Right. The count itself dropped, and two is still at the minimum, so the group has nothing to launch.

choices.text: Desired stays at 3 and a replacement launches
choices.why: That is --no-should-decrement-desired-capacity, the form the lesson used to show a replacement.

choices.text: Desired falls to 2, and the minimum makes the group launch one more anyway
choices.why: Two is the minimum, not below it; the group is satisfied.

choices.text: The call is refused, because the group would fall below its minimum
choices.why: It would be refused at a desired of 2, where decrementing goes below the minimum. At 3 it does not.

prompt: Which of these did moto 5.2.3 do differently from AWS in this lesson? Choose all that apply.
hint: Four of the six were called out in the prose as moto's.

choices.text: It accepted a desired capacity above the maximum
choices.why: AWS refuses that with a ValidationError.

choices.text: It printed nothing when create-auto-scaling-group worked
choices.why: AWS prints nothing either; a successful create has no output.

choices.text: It put every instance into the first subnet
choices.why: AWS spreads a group over the zones of its subnets.

choices.text: It left an instance marked unhealthy running
choices.why: AWS terminates and replaces it.

choices.text: It wrote the aws:autoscaling:groupName tag on each instance
choices.why: AWS writes the same tag; it is how the group's instances are found.

choices.text: It ignored --source-version
choices.why: AWS builds the new version from the source and the data sent beside it.

prompt: What does a group whose minimum, desired and maximum are all 1 give you?
hint: It cannot scale. What else does a group do?

choices.text: Nothing beyond a plain instance, since it can never scale
choices.why: Scaling is one thing a group does. Keeping its count, by replacing what fails, is the other, and that still works at one.

choices.text: An instance the group will never terminate, which makes it safe for state
choices.why: The group terminates it as soon as it fails a check. Nothing on it is safe from that.

choices.text: One instance in each zone of its subnets
choices.why: Three subnets with a desired of 1 is still one instance, in one of the zones.

choices.text: One instance that is replaced when it fails its checks
choices.why: Right. It is the cheapest way to have a single server come back on its own, provided nothing on it must survive.
